title: Grade 4 ENGLISH LANGUAGE — 2.4.1 Writing: Creative Writing

pages.lesson:
PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

An open-ended composition is a story you build from a topic or a beginning, while you choose how it ends. In this sub-strand you will gather ideas, put events in order, write in clear paragraphs, and proof-read so a reader can follow and enjoy your story.

## Strand 2.0: Family Celebrations
Sub-strand 2.4.1: Writing: Creative Writing
Suggested lessons: 3

## What this sub-strand covers
• Open ended Compositions

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 English Language Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Theme 2.0 Family Celebrations, Sub-strand 2.4.1 Creative Writing

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) express relevant ideas on a given topic for effective communication
b) write an open ended composition creatively for self-expression
c) realise the importance of creativity in writing for effective communication

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why is it necessary to express thoughts and feelings clearly?
2. How can you make your story interesting?

PAGE 2: How we will learn

## Learning experiences
• discuss how to write a story on a given topic together
• talk about the possible order of events in a given story with peers
• write the first paragraph of a composition while observing the correct punctuation and spelling
• write the whole composition legibly, neatly, and independently
• proof-read compositions with peers
• collaborate with peers to share their completed stories
• search and read written compositions online or offline

## Core competencies
• Creativity and Imagination: This is nurtured as the learner explores creative ideas to talk about the possible order of events in a given story with peers.
• Digital Literacy: This is developed as the learner interacts with digital devices to search for resources on guided compositions online.

## Values
• Integrity: This is developed as the learner puts in effort to complete own compositions independently.
• Responsibility: This is enhanced as the learner takes up allocated tasks to search and read written compositions online or offline

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Social Cohesion: This is developed as the learner fosters tolerance and respect for one another during group activities.

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner is able to connect the aspect of guided composition writing to their learning in Kiswahili.

PAGE 3: Lesson 1: Ideas and the order of events

LESSON 1: IDEAS AND THE ORDER OF EVENTS
=======================================

## What you will learn
• Collect ideas that fit a celebration topic.
• Arrange events in a beginning, a middle and an ending.
• Choose an ending of your own for an open-ended story.

Curriculum outcomes: a) express relevant ideas on a given topic for effective communication

## Introduction
A story that jumps from a cake to a prize to a stranger, with no link, leaves the reader behind. Before you write sentences, you need ideas that belong together and an order that a listener can follow.

PAGE 4: Lesson 1: Ideas and the order of events — Relevant ideas

## Notes

### What open-ended means
Sometimes the teacher gives a topic, such as "A birthday I will not forget", or the first sentences of a story. The ending is not supplied. You decide what happens last. That is an open-ended composition. Your ending must still grow out of the events you have already chosen. A surprise is welcome. A surprise that forgets the rest of the story is not.

### Relevant ideas
Relevant ideas fit the topic. For a family celebration, useful ideas include who is there, what you are celebrating, what you see and hear, a small problem, and how people feel.

Less useful ideas, unless you tie them in, are a football score from another day or a list of every food you have ever eaten. Ask: does this idea help the reader understand this celebration?

Speak your ideas before you write them. A partner can say, "I do not yet know why the lights matter." Then you add the reason.

PAGE 5: Lesson 1: Ideas and the order of events — Order

### Order
Most Grade 4 stories need three parts.

1. Beginning: who, where and when. The reader meets the family and the celebration.
2. Middle: what happens, including a problem or a surprise.
3. Ending: how the problem is solved, and how people feel. This part is yours to decide.

Here is a plan, not yet a full story.

- Beginning: Our family meets on Saturday to celebrate Grandmother's birthday. Balloons are up. The cake is on the table.
- Middle: The lights go out. The little children are afraid. My brother finds a lamp. My sister starts a song.
- Ending I might choose: Grandmother says the singing was her best gift. Or: a neighbour brings more lamps and we cut the cake outside.

Both endings fit. Write one, not both, so the story has a single path.

PAGE 6: Lesson 1: Ideas and the order of events — Feelings and clear thoughts

### Feelings and clear thoughts
Readers remember feelings. "I was proud" tells more than "It was nice". Name the feeling and the reason: I was proud because my sister's song kept the little children calm.

Talk the order aloud: first, next, then, finally. If you cannot tell it in that chain, you are not ready to write paragraphs.

## Key words
• open-ended — having an ending that the writer is free to decide
• relevant — connected to the topic and useful for it
• composition — a piece of writing, such as a story, made of paragraphs

PAGE 7: Lesson 1: Ideas and the order of events — Example 1

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which idea is relevant to a story about a wedding: the bride's song, or a list of rivers in the country?

Working:
1. The topic is a wedding.
2. A song at the wedding belongs in the story.
3. A list of rivers does not help the reader understand the wedding unless the story is about a river, which it is not.

Answer: The bride's song is relevant.

## Worked examples

### Example 2
Put these events in story order: we cut the cake; the guests arrived; I wrote my aunt's name on a card.

Working:
1. The card is prepared before the guests are there.
2. Guests arrive before the cake is cut.
3. Cutting the cake is a later event.

Answer: I wrote my aunt's name on a card; the guests arrived; we cut the cake.

PAGE 8: Lesson 1: Ideas and the order of events — Plan the path of a story

## Activity: Plan the path of a story
You will need: Paper, Pencils

1. In a group, choose one topic: a birthday, a wedding or a graduation in a family.

2. Each person says two ideas that fit the topic. The group sets aside any idea that does not fit.

3. Agree on a beginning, a middle with one problem, and two possible endings.

4. Each learner chooses one ending and tells the whole plan aloud using first, next, then and finally.

## Practice

1. What does open-ended mean for a composition?

2. Name the three parts of a simple story plan.

3. Why is a list of every food you have ever eaten a weak idea for one birthday story?

4. Give a relevant ending for a story in which the lights go out at a birthday party.

PAGE 9: Lesson 1: Ideas and the order of events — Answers to practice

## Answers to practice

1. The writer chooses how the story ends.

2. Beginning, middle and ending.

3. Most of those foods are not part of this celebration, so they do not help the reader follow the story.

4. Any fitting ending, for example: My brother found a lamp and we sang until Grandmother laughed.

## Summary
• Keep ideas that belong to the topic.
• Plan a beginning, a middle and one ending.
• An open ending must still follow from the events.

LESSON 2: WRITING THE COMPOSITION
=================================

## What you will learn
• Write a first paragraph with correct capitals and full stops.
• Complete an open-ended story in neat paragraphs.
• Use interesting words without losing the order of events.

Curriculum outcomes: b) write an open ended composition creatively for self-expression

## Introduction
A plan is a path. Paragraphs are the steps you take on that path. The first paragraph opens the door. The last paragraph closes it in a way you have chosen.

PAGE 10: Lesson 2: Writing the composition — The first paragraph

## Notes

### The first paragraph
The opening tells who, where and when, and hints at the celebration. Keep it short.

Model opening:

On Saturday our family held a small party for Grandmother. We had decorated the room with balloons and a long red ribbon. A cake sat in the middle of the table, and the children kept glancing at it.

Check the opening before you continue:

- Each sentence begins with a capital letter.
- Each sentence ends with a full stop, a question mark or an exclamation mark. Do not sprinkle exclamation marks on every line.
- Names of people and the word I take capitals.
- Spelling of celebration words is steady: birthday, balloon, ribbon, cake, guests.

PAGE 11: Lesson 2: Writing the composition — The middle and the ending

### The middle and the ending
Write the problem in the middle. Show what people do. Then write one ending.

Model story, The Surprise Song:

On Saturday our family held a small party for Grandmother. We had decorated the room with balloons and a long red ribbon. A cake sat in the middle of the table.

In the middle of the songs, the lights went out. The little children went quiet. My brother found a lamp, and my sister started a new song. Soon everyone was singing again, and Grandmother laughed.

I was proud of my family. We did not let a small problem spoil the day. Grandmother said it was her best party because we had stayed together.

That model is complete so you can see the shape. Your own story should not copy it. Use a new opening, given below, and choose your own middle and ending.

PAGE 12: Lesson 2: Writing the composition — Make it interesting and still clear

### Your opening
"The balloons were ready and the cake was on the table. Then we heard a knock at the door."

Decide who knocks, what they bring or what they need, and how the celebration ends. Write at least three paragraphs: this beginning, a middle, and your ending.

### Make it interesting and still clear
- Use one simile if it truly fits: The ribbon was as red as a ripe tomato.
- Use speaking: "Come in," said Mother.
- Name a feeling and its cause.
- Keep first, next and finally in that order even if you do not write those exact words.

Write in print, on the lines, with a margin. Neat writing is part of the gift you give the reader. Finish the whole composition yourself. A partner may talk about ideas, but the sentences should be yours.

PAGE 13: Lesson 2: Writing the composition — Example 1

## Key words
• paragraph — a group of sentences about one part of the story
• opening — the first paragraph, which introduces the story
• margin — the empty space at the edge of the page

## Worked examples

### Example 1
What is missing in this opening? "on saturday we had a party the cake was sweet"

Working:
1. Sentences need capital letters.
2. Each sentence needs a full stop.
3. Saturday is a name of a day, so it needs a capital.

Answer: On Saturday we had a party. The cake was sweet.

## Worked examples

### Example 2
Why should your story use the given opening but not copy The Surprise Song?

Working:
1. The model shows the shape of a composition.
2. An open-ended story asks for your own events and ending.
3. Copying the model is not your own composition.

Answer: The model teaches the shape. The sentences and the ending should be your own.

PAGE 14: Lesson 2: Writing the composition — Write the whole story

## Activity: Write the whole story
You will need: Exercise book, Pen or pencil

1. Talk with a partner about who might knock at the door in the given opening, and what could happen next.

2. Write the first paragraph only. Check capitals, full stops and spelling before you go on.

3. Write the middle and your own ending in further paragraphs.

4. Read the whole composition aloud softly to hear whether the events follow one another.

## Practice

1. Rewrite with correct punctuation: my sister sang a song then the lights went out

2. What three things should the first paragraph help the reader know?

3. Name one way to make a celebration story interesting.

4. Why do you write only one ending?

PAGE 15: Lesson 2: Writing the composition — Answers to practice

## Answers to practice

1. My sister sang a song. Then the lights went out.

2. Who is in the story, where they are, and when it happens. It should also show that there is a celebration.

3. Any one: use a simile, use speech, name a feeling, or include a small problem.

4. So the story follows one clear path that the reader can finish.

## Summary
• Open with who, where and when, in correct sentences.
• Write a middle and one ending of your own.
• Interesting words still need a clear order.

LESSON 3: PROOF-READING AND SHARING
===================================

## What you will learn
• Proof-read a composition for punctuation, spelling and order.
• Share a finished story and listen to another learner's story.
• Explain why creative writing is worth the effort.

Curriculum outcomes: b) write an open ended composition creatively for self-expression; c) realise the importance of creativity in writing for effective communication

## Introduction
A strong idea can hide inside weak sentences. Proof-reading is the quiet work that lets the idea out. You read as if you have never seen the story before.

PAGE 16: Lesson 3: Proof-reading and sharing — What proof-reading means

## Notes

### What proof-reading means
To proof-read is to check finished writing for mistakes and for sense. You are not starting a new story. You are making this one clear.

Use a short list. Touch each item with your pencil as you check it.

- Does the story fit the topic?
- Are the events in an order a stranger could follow?
- Does each sentence begin with a capital letter and end with a full stop or another correct mark?
- Are names and I capitalised?
- Are celebration words spelled the same way each time?
- Is the handwriting on the lines, with spaces between words?
- Does the ending match the events, and is it your own?

Mark a mistake lightly and write the correction above it or in the margin, as your teacher prefers. Do not cover the word with a dark scribble.

PAGE 17: Lesson 3: Proof-reading and sharing — Read with a partner

### Read with a partner
Read your partner's story once for enjoyment and once for the list. Say one thing that worked: "I could picture the ribbon." Then say one improvement: "The second paragraph needs a full stop after song."

Accept the same help on your own page. Integrity here means you do the writing yourself and you also tell the truth about a mistake. Copying a friend's paragraphs is not creativity.

### Why creativity matters
A report can say, "We had a party." A creative story makes the reader hear the song and feel the dark room when the lights fail. That is self-expression: your thoughts and feelings become something another person can understand.

Clear creative writing is also kind. The reader does not have to guess your ending or decode your spelling. When thoughts are easy to follow, communication works.

PAGE 18: Lesson 3: Proof-reading and sharing — Example 1

### Learning from other stories
With your teacher, look at one or two compositions written for children, in a book or on a site the teacher opens. Notice the opening, the problem and the ending. Do not copy their sentences. Borrow the shape if it helps you, then close the page and return to your own words.

When you share, speak clearly, hold the book still, and stop at the end. Listeners tell the writer the part they remember. If several people remember the same event, that event was well written.

## Key words
• proof-read — to check writing for mistakes and for sense
• self-expression — showing your own thoughts and feelings
• correction — the right form written in place of a mistake

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A story ends with a football final that was never mentioned before. What should the writer change?

Working:
1. Check whether the ending matches the events.
2. A celebration story needs an ending about that celebration.
3. Replace the unrelated ending or add events that truly lead to it. The first choice is usually better.

Answer: Change the ending so it follows from the celebration, or rebuild the story so the match truly belongs. Do not leave a surprise that forgets the topic.

PAGE 19: Lesson 3: Proof-reading and sharing — Proof-read and share

## Worked examples

### Example 2
Your partner wrote "the guests was happy." What do you say, kindly and clearly?

Working:
1. Point to the useful part first if you can.
2. Then name the grammar: guests is plural, so the verb is were.

Answer: I enjoyed the party scene. Please change "was" to "were", because guests is plural: the guests were happy.

## Activity: Proof-read and share
You will need: Your finished composition, A pencil, A book or a teacher-chosen page of a sample story

1. Proof-read your composition with the checklist in this lesson.

2. Exchange books with a partner. Point out one success and one correction.

3. Write a neat final copy if your teacher asks for it.

4. Read the stories aloud to the group. Listeners name the event they remember.

5. With the teacher, look at one other composition in print or on a screen and notice its opening and ending. Do not copy it.

PAGE 20: Lesson 3: Proof-reading and sharing — Answers to practice

## Practice

1. Name four things to check when you proof-read.

2. Correct the sentence: the guests was happy

3. Why is copying a friend's story not creative writing?

4. What is one reason to write a story creatively instead of only saying "We had a party"?

## Answers to practice

1. Any four: topic, order of events, capital letters, full stops, spelling, neat writing, and whether the ending fits.

2. The guests were happy.

3. Creative writing expresses your own ideas and ending. A copied story is someone else's work.

4. The reader can picture the events and understand your thoughts and feelings.

## Summary
• Proof-read for order, punctuation, spelling and a fitting ending.
• Tell a partner one success and one clear correction.
• Your own ideas, written clearly, are what make the story creative.

PAGE 21: Revision quiz

REVISION QUIZ
=============

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. What is an open-ended composition?
   A. A story whose ending is copied from a book
   B. A story in which the writer chooses the ending
   C. A list of spelling words
   D. A form with blank lines

2. Which idea is relevant to a birthday story?
   A. Grandmother laughed when the song began
   B. A list of all the rivers in the country
   C. The price of a bus from last year
   D. A page of multiplication tables

3. Which order is best?
   A. Ending, middle, beginning
   B. Middle, beginning, ending
   C. Beginning, middle, ending
   D. Ending, beginning, middle

4. Which opening is punctuated correctly?
   A. on saturday we had a party
   B. On Saturday we had a party.
   C. On saturday we had a party
   D. on Saturday we had a party.

5. What should the first paragraph help the reader know?

6. Why should a story have one ending rather than two?

7. Which correction is right?
   A. the guests was happy → The guests was happy.
   B. the guests was happy → The guests were happy.
   C. the guests was happy → the guests were happy
   D. the guests was happy → The guest were happy.

8. What does it mean to proof-read?
   A. To start a different story
   B. To check writing for mistakes and sense
   C. To draw a new cover
   D. To memorise every word of a poem

9. Why does creativity matter in a story?

10. A partner's story is enjoyable but the ending is about a different topic. What should you tell them?

PAGE 22: Quiz answers

ANSWERS
=======

1. B. A story in which the writer chooses the ending
   The writer decides how the story finishes, while keeping it connected to the events.

2. A. Grandmother laughed when the song began
   Grandmother's reaction belongs to the celebration.

3. C. Beginning, middle, ending
   Readers meet the people, then the events, then the close.

4. B. On Saturday we had a party.
   The sentence starts with a capital, Saturday has a capital, and it ends with a full stop.

5. Who is involved, where they are, and when the story happens.
   The opening sets the scene before the problem.

6. So the reader can follow one clear path to the finish.
   Two endings leave the story unfinished or confusing.

7. B. the guests was happy → The guests were happy.
   The sentence needs a capital letter, and a plural subject takes were.

8. B. To check writing for mistakes and sense
   Proof-reading improves the piece you have already written.

9. It lets the reader picture events and understand the writer's thoughts and feelings.
   A bare statement such as "We had a party" gives much less.

10. The story is enjoyable, and the ending should be changed so it follows the celebration.
   Say what works, then give one clear improvement.

• Keep ideas that belong to the topic.
• Plan a beginning, a middle and one ending.
• An open ending must still follow from the events.

LESSON 2: WRITING THE COMPOSITION
=================================

## What you will learn
• Write a first paragraph with correct capitals and full stops.
• Complete an open-ended story in neat paragraphs.
• Use interesting words without losing the order of events.

Curriculum outcomes: b) write an open ended composition creatively for self-expression

## Introduction
A plan is a path. Paragraphs are the steps you take on that path. The first paragraph opens the door. The last paragraph closes it in a way you have chosen.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Writing the composition — The first paragraph
studyPages.body:
## Notes

### The first paragraph
The opening tells who, where and when, and hints at the celebration. Keep it short.

Model opening:

On Saturday our family held a small party for Grandmother. We had decorated the room with balloons and a long red ribbon. A cake sat in the middle of the table, and the children kept glancing at it.

Check the opening before you continue:

- Each sentence begins with a capital letter.
- Each sentence ends with a full stop, a question mark or an exclamation mark. Do not sprinkle exclamation marks on every line.
- Names of people and the word I take capitals.
- Spelling of celebration words is steady: birthday, balloon, ribbon, cake, guests.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Writing the composition — The middle and the ending
studyPages.body:
### The middle and the ending
Write the problem in the middle. Show what people do. Then write one ending.

Model story, The Surprise Song:

On Saturday our family held a small party for Grandmother. We had decorated the room with balloons and a long red ribbon. A cake sat in the middle of the table.

In the middle of the songs, the lights went out. The little children went quiet. My brother found a lamp, and my sister started a new song. Soon everyone was singing again, and Grandmother laughed.

I was proud of my family. We did not let a small problem spoil the day. Grandmother said it was her best party because we had stayed together.

That model is complete so you can see the shape. Your own story should not copy it. Use a new opening, given below, and choose your own middle and ending.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Writing the composition — Make it interesting and still clear
studyPages.body:
### Your opening
"The balloons were ready and the cake was on the table. Then we heard a knock at the door."

Decide who knocks, what they bring or what they need, and how the celebration ends. Write at least three paragraphs: this beginning, a middle, and your ending.

### Make it interesting and still clear
- Use one simile if it truly fits: The ribbon was as red as a ripe tomato.
- Use speaking: "Come in," said Mother.
- Name a feeling and its cause.
- Keep first, next and finally in that order even if you do not write those exact words.

Write in print, on the lines, with a margin. Neat writing is part of the gift you give the reader. Finish the whole composition yourself. A partner may talk about ideas, but the sentences should be yours.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Writing the composition — Example 1
studyPages.body:
## Key words
• paragraph — a group of sentences about one part of the story
• opening — the first paragraph, which introduces the story
• margin — the empty space at the edge of the page

## Worked examples

### Example 1
What is missing in this opening? "on saturday we had a party the cake was sweet"

Working:
1. Sentences need capital letters.
2. Each sentence needs a full stop.
3. Saturday is a name of a day, so it needs a capital.

Answer: On Saturday we had a party. The cake was sweet.

## Worked examples

### Example 2
Why should your story use the given opening but not copy The Surprise Song?

Working:
1. The model shows the shape of a composition.
2. An open-ended story asks for your own events and ending.
3. Copying the model is not your own composition.

Answer: The model teaches the shape. The sentences and the ending should be your own.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Writing the composition — Write the whole story
studyPages.body:
## Activity: Write the whole story
You will need: Exercise book, Pen or pencil

1. Talk with a partner about who might knock at the door in the given opening, and what could happen next.

2. Write the first paragraph only. Check capitals, full stops and spelling before you go on.

3. Write the middle and your own ending in further paragraphs.

4. Read the whole composition aloud softly to hear whether the events follow one another.

## Practice

1. Rewrite with correct punctuation: my sister sang a song then the lights went out

2. What three things should the first paragraph help the reader know?

3. Name one way to make a celebration story interesting.

4. Why do you write only one ending?

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Writing the composition — Answers to practice
studyPages.body:
## Answers to practice

1. My sister sang a song. Then the lights went out.

2. Who is in the story, where they are, and when it happens. It should also show that there is a celebration.

3. Any one: use a simile, use speech, name a feeling, or include a small problem.

4. So the story follows one clear path that the reader can finish.

## Summary
• Open with who, where and when, in correct sentences.
• Write a middle and one ending of your own.
• Interesting words still need a clear order.

LESSON 3: PROOF-READING AND SHARING
===================================

## What you will learn
• Proof-read a composition for punctuation, spelling and order.
• Share a finished story and listen to another learner's story.
• Explain why creative writing is worth the effort.

Curriculum outcomes: b) write an open ended composition creatively for self-expression; c) realise the importance of creativity in writing for effective communication

## Introduction
A strong idea can hide inside weak sentences. Proof-reading is the quiet work that lets the idea out. You read as if you have never seen the story before.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Proof-reading and sharing — What proof-reading means
studyPages.body:
## Notes

### What proof-reading means
To proof-read is to check finished writing for mistakes and for sense. You are not starting a new story. You are making this one clear.

Use a short list. Touch each item with your pencil as you check it.

- Does the story fit the topic?
- Are the events in an order a stranger could follow?
- Does each sentence begin with a capital letter and end with a full stop or another correct mark?
- Are names and I capitalised?
- Are celebration words spelled the same way each time?
- Is the handwriting on the lines, with spaces between words?
- Does the ending match the events, and is it your own?

Mark a mistake lightly and write the correction above it or in the margin, as your teacher prefers. Do not cover the word with a dark scribble.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Proof-reading and sharing — Read with a partner
studyPages.body:
### Read with a partner
Read your partner's story once for enjoyment and once for the list. Say one thing that worked: "I could picture the ribbon." Then say one improvement: "The second paragraph needs a full stop after song."

Accept the same help on your own page. Integrity here means you do the writing yourself and you also tell the truth about a mistake. Copying a friend's paragraphs is not creativity.

### Why creativity matters
A report can say, "We had a party." A creative story makes the reader hear the song and feel the dark room when the lights fail. That is self-expression: your thoughts and feelings become something another person can understand.

Clear creative writing is also kind. The reader does not have to guess your ending or decode your spelling. When thoughts are easy to follow, communication works.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Proof-reading and sharing — Example 1
studyPages.body:
### Learning from other stories
With your teacher, look at one or two compositions written for children, in a book or on a site the teacher opens. Notice the opening, the problem and the ending. Do not copy their sentences. Borrow the shape if it helps you, then close the page and return to your own words.

When you share, speak clearly, hold the book still, and stop at the end. Listeners tell the writer the part they remember. If several people remember the same event, that event was well written.

## Key words
• proof-read — to check writing for mistakes and for sense
• self-expression — showing your own thoughts and feelings
• correction — the right form written in place of a mistake

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A story ends with a football final that was never mentioned before. What should the writer change?

Working:
1. Check whether the ending matches the events.
2. A celebration story needs an ending about that celebration.
3. Replace the unrelated ending or add events that truly lead to it. The first choice is usually better.

Answer: Change the ending so it follows from the celebration, or rebuild the story so the match truly belongs. Do not leave a surprise that forgets the topic.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Proof-reading and sharing — Proof-read and share
studyPages.body:
## Worked examples

### Example 2
Your partner wrote "the guests was happy." What do you say, kindly and clearly?

Working:
1. Point to the useful part first if you can.
2. Then name the grammar: guests is plural, so the verb is were.

Answer: I enjoyed the party scene. Please change "was" to "were", because guests is plural: the guests were happy.

## Activity: Proof-read and share
You will need: Your finished composition, A pencil, A book or a teacher-chosen page of a sample story

1. Proof-read your composition with the checklist in this lesson.

2. Exchange books with a partner. Point out one success and one correction.

3. Write a neat final copy if your teacher asks for it.

4. Read the stories aloud to the group. Listeners name the event they remember.

5. With the teacher, look at one other composition in print or on a screen and notice its opening and ending. Do not copy it.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Proof-reading and sharing — Answers to practice
studyPages.body:
## Practice

1. Name four things to check when you proof-read.

2. Correct the sentence: the guests was happy

3. Why is copying a friend's story not creative writing?

4. What is one reason to write a story creatively instead of only saying "We had a party"?

## Answers to practice

1. Any four: topic, order of events, capital letters, full stops, spelling, neat writing, and whether the ending fits.

2. The guests were happy.

3. Creative writing expresses your own ideas and ending. A copied story is someone else's work.

4. The reader can picture the events and understand your thoughts and feelings.

## Summary
• Proof-read for order, punctuation, spelling and a fitting ending.
• Tell a partner one success and one clear correction.
• Your own ideas, written clearly, are what make the story creative.

studyPages.title: Revision quiz
studyPages.body:
REVISION QUIZ
=============

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. What is an open-ended composition?
   A. A story whose ending is copied from a book
   B. A story in which the writer chooses the ending
   C. A list of spelling words
   D. A form with blank lines

2. Which idea is relevant to a birthday story?
   A. Grandmother laughed when the song began
   B. A list of all the rivers in the country
   C. The price of a bus from last year
   D. A page of multiplication tables

3. Which order is best?
   A. Ending, middle, beginning
   B. Middle, beginning, ending
   C. Beginning, middle, ending
   D. Ending, beginning, middle

4. Which opening is punctuated correctly?
   A. on saturday we had a party
   B. On Saturday we had a party.
   C. On saturday we had a party
   D. on Saturday we had a party.

5. What should the first paragraph help the reader know?

6. Why should a story have one ending rather than two?

7. Which correction is right?
   A. the guests was happy → The guests was happy.
   B. the guests was happy → The guests were happy.
   C. the guests was happy → the guests were happy
   D. the guests was happy → The guest were happy.

8. What does it mean to proof-read?
   A. To start a different story
   B. To check writing for mistakes and sense
   C. To draw a new cover
   D. To memorise every word of a poem

9. Why does creativity matter in a story?

10. A partner's story is enjoyable but the ending is about a different topic. What should you tell them?

studyPages.title: Quiz answers
studyPages.body:
ANSWERS
=======

1. B. A story in which the writer chooses the ending
   The writer decides how the story finishes, while keeping it connected to the events.

2. A. Grandmother laughed when the song began
   Grandmother's reaction belongs to the celebration.

3. C. Beginning, middle, ending
   Readers meet the people, then the events, then the close.

4. B. On Saturday we had a party.
   The sentence starts with a capital, Saturday has a capital, and it ends with a full stop.

5. Who is involved, where they are, and when the story happens.
   The opening sets the scene before the problem.

6. So the reader can follow one clear path to the finish.
   Two endings leave the story unfinished or confusing.

7. B. the guests was happy → The guests were happy.
   The sentence needs a capital letter, and a plural subject takes were.

8. B. To check writing for mistakes and sense
   Proof-reading improves the piece you have already written.

9. It lets the reader picture events and understand the writer's thoughts and feelings.
   A bare statement such as "We had a party" gives much less.

10. The story is enjoyable, and the ending should be changed so it follows the celebration.
   Say what works, then give one clear improvement.
